growth_story.headline: Micronesia's income per person has grown about 0.7 percent a year since 1990, carried by US Compact grants and set back by cuts, closures and emigration.
growth_story.arc: The data show one long era since 1990: income per person in the Federated States of Micronesia grew 0.7 percent a year on average from 1990 to 2025, from about $2,394 to about $3,020 in constant dollars. Within that era the pace was 0.1 percent a year in 2006–2015 and 0.5 percent in 2016–2025, and in 2025 income per person was 0.8 percent below its 2019 peak and about where it first stood in 2011. The sources tie this slow pace to an economy built on US grants under the Compact of Free Association: government spending is the main source of income, and the private sector mostly serves the public sector. The sharp falls came when that support was cut or stalled, in the late 1990s and again around 2014, and when the borders stayed shut from March 2020 to September 2022. The Compact has since been renewed with larger grants, but the sources describe slow use of the money, limited capacity and sustained emigration, and the IMF sees medium-term growth prospects as subdued.

threads.title: An economy run on grants
threads.text: US grants under the Compact of Free Association pay for most government spending, and that spending is the main source of income for the rest of the economy. The private sector has yet to become the engine of growth and mostly serves the public sector.

threads.title: Grant cuts and stalled projects
threads.text: Income per person fell 3.8 percent in 1996 and 6.5 percent in 1997. With Compact grants being reduced, the government set out from 1997 to cut the cost of its operations. It fell again in 2012, 2013 and 2014, by up to 3.9 percent a year, as building projects moved slowly and Compact infrastructure grants for new projects were suspended; over 2010–2019, investment in buildings and equipment pulled growth down rather than lifting it.

threads.title: A long border closure
threads.text: The country kept its borders shut from March 2020 to September 2022, one of the longest closures in the world, which cut trade, tourism and the arrival of workers and equipment for building projects. Income per person fell 2.6 percent in 2020, rose 2.4 percent in 2021 and fell 3.5 percent in 2022; the IMF describes the 2021 recovery as short-lived.

threads.text: Because the Compact lets citizens live and work in the United States, many young people leave. The IMF links this steady outflow to labour shortages and sees medium-term growth prospects as subdued.

since_last_year.text: In the data, income per person grew 1.8 percent in 2024 and 0.6 percent in 2025. The World Bank reports that Typhoon Sinlaku damaged infrastructure and crops and further slowed public building work, while higher world oil prices have raised the cost of imports. The IMF and the World Bank both expect growth to slow in the 2026 fiscal year.

growth_story.tension: The sources stress steady emigration. If emigration shrinks the population, income per person would grow faster than the economy as a whole. Yet in the data, income per person grew more slowly in 2024 and 2025 than the total growth the World Bank and IMF report for those years. Part of the gap may come from fiscal years, which end in September, and part from uncertain population estimates for a small country whose people move freely.
